title: Ground stop proves "we have to get off old network," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says
summary: On Face the Nation, Margaret Brennan presses Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Friday's nationwide FAA ground stop, which cancelled well over a thousand flights and left aircraft and crews scattered across the country. Duffy traces the failure to work by contractor L3Harris on a router and an aging copper telecom line in Arkansas, rejects a union's account of what went wrong, and argues the episode shows the FAA must abandon a decades-old network. Brennan challenges him with a GAO warning about speed versus cost and Democrats' claim that most of the money already approved sits unspent, while Duffy insists the funds are committed to radar and radio contracts and confirms he wants about $50 billion in total from Congress.
focus: Shadow Duffy's early explanation of why planes and crews are stranded and how airlines must carefully plan the restart, then the fast funding exchange near the end where he distinguishes money that is committed from money that is spent, which is great practice for numbers and contract language.

vocab.context: Duffy explained that airlines need time to carefully coordinate getting planes and crews back into normal service.
vocab.example: The integration office choreographed the system cutover so that no customer region went dark at the same time.

vocab.meaning: to officially take equipment or a facility out of service
vocab.context: Duffy said the old copper line at the Arkansas site was due to be retired and replaced with fibre.
vocab.example: We recommend decommissioning the two legacy data centres once the cloud migration passes its final stress test.

vocab.meaning: having received less money or resources than needed over time
vocab.context: Duffy argued that air traffic control infrastructure has gone without adequate funding for years.
vocab.example: The diligence team flagged the target's IT stack as badly underinvested, so we built a catch-up capex line into the model.

vocab.meaning: (of public money) to formally commit funds to a specific contract or purpose, even if not yet paid out
vocab.context: Duffy pushed back on claims of unspent money by saying the funds were already committed to radar and radio contracts.
vocab.example: Most of the grant has been obligated to vendors, but actual cash outflows will not peak until the second half of next year.

vocab.meaning: moving budgeted money from one use to another within the same funding
vocab.context: Brennan asked whether shifting existing funds to other priorities could cover the FAA's needs.
vocab.example: Rather than request new budget, the CFO proposed a reprogramming of unused marketing funds into the pricing project.

vocab.context: Duffy described faulty data spreading into the system and overwhelming the FAA's network.

vocab.context: Duffy said some delays persisted in parts of the controlled sky even as flights resumed.

vocab.context: Duffy said radar systems cannot simply be bought ready-made, which is why delivery takes time.

vocab.context: Duffy said similar daytime upgrades at remote sites had been done many times with no trouble.

vocab.meaning: to change from one system or method to another
vocab.context: Duffy used it when describing how hundreds of radios and copper lines had been moved to new technology.

vocab.context: Brennan asked whether the FAA had been surprised by the failure.

phrases.meaning: making good progress towards a goal
phrases.context: Duffy said recovery from the disruption was progressing and full schedules would soon return.
phrases.example: With three of five plants converted, we are well on the way to the cost-reduction target.

phrases.context: Duffy said he was trying to persuade Congress and the public that a new network was needed.
phrases.example: To make the case for the acquisition, we need hard numbers on revenue synergies, not just strategic fit.

phrases.context: Brennan summarised a GAO finding that the FAA was moving fast while accepting uncertainty over costs.
phrases.example: They pushed the launch forward at the risk of a weaker product, betting that being first mattered more.

phrases.context: Duffy framed halting all air traffic as a rare measure used only when safety demanded it.
phrases.example: The board took the extraordinary step of suspending guidance until the audit was complete.
